overview: Banco Santander (Brasil) S.A. is one of Brazil's largest private-sector banks by assets, offering retail and commercial banking, consumer finance/auto lending, corporate and wholesale banking, insurance, cards, and asset management/brokerage across Brazil. It is roughly 89-90% owned by Spain's Banco Santander S.A. (through Sterrebeeck B.V. and Grupo Empresarial Santander, S.L.), with the remainder held as free-floating units/ADRs on the NYSE (BSBR) and B3 (SANB11); each NYSE ADR represents one unit composed of one common and one preferred share. As a Brazilian IFRS filer that reports annually on Form 20-F as a foreign private issuer, its USD-denominated ADR sits atop BRL-denominated earnings and equity, creating direct translation exposure for US investors.

business_model.summary: Santander Brasil earns a net interest margin spread by taking deposits/funding and lending to individuals, SMEs and corporates, supplemented by fee income from cards, insurance, asset management, 'consórcios' (installment purchase clubs) and brokerage. Profitability is highly geared to the Selic policy rate: a large 'Market NII' book captures/loses money on interest-rate positioning, while 'Client NII' is driven by loan volume, mix and spread. Consumer finance (vehicle financing, ~20% market share of the individual vehicle-financing portfolio, done via dealer/automaker partnerships including a JV with Hyundai and a tie-up with PSA/Stellantis dealers) is a structurally higher-margin, more digital franchise and management calls it the 'largest and most digital Consumer Finance platform' in Brazil.

revenue_streams.name: Net interest income (client + market NII)
revenue_streams.trend: pressured - client NII growing on volume/mix but market NII swinging to losses on rate sensitivity

revenue_streams.name: Fees and commissions (cards, insurance, asset management, consórcios, brokerage, current account)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - management's explicit diversification pillar, ~4-7% YoY ex-reclassification effects

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (individuals/mass-market, high-income 'Select' segment) and B2B (SMEs, corporates/wholesale); ~76 million total customers (~34 million active) as of mid-2026, trailing Nubank (~115 million) and Bradesco/Itau in raw customer count but competing on wallet share, asset base (~$255bn) and primary-relationship depth rather than headline user count
business_model.geographic_mix: Brazil only (domestic bank subsidiary of a global group); BRL-denominated financials, USD-denominated ADR

competitive_position.market_position: Fifth-largest Brazilian bank by assets (~$255bn) behind Itau, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil and Caixa; the top five banks control roughly 80% of system assets. By customer count Santander (~71-76 million) now trails Nubank (which surpassed Bradesco in early 2026 to become Brazil's second-largest institution by customers, ~115 million, >60% of Brazil's adult population) as well as Bradesco (~110 million) and Itau (~101 million) -- Santander is the smallest of the traditional 'big five' by headcount of customers, though it remains a top-five player by balance sheet and retains leadership in individual vehicle financing (~20% share).

moat_factors.description: Access to the global Santander technology platform, risk-management expertise, cross-border products for multinational/SME clients, and capital support from a AA-rated-adjacent global banking group lowers funding and technology costs versus standalone domestic peers.

Brazilian banking requires Banco Central do Brasil (BACEN) licensing, large capital bases (CET1 ~11-12%, BIS ~15%) and branch/agent networks (916 stores, >26,000 shared ATMs) that are costly to replicate, though digital challengers have eroded this advantage in payments and unsecured consumer credit.

Partnerships with six of Brazil's ten largest automakers and a dealer-embedded origination model give Santander Financiamentos a durable ~20% share of individual vehicle financing with high satisfaction (NPS ~90) and fast (four-click) onboarding.

Strategy is explicitly built around deepening 'primary relationship' status (current account, cards, payroll, investments) to raise transactionality and cross-sell, which raises switching costs versus a single-product fintech relationship.
Santander is a recognized global brand, but in Brazil brand loyalty is weaker than for Itau/Bradesco among legacy savers and weaker than Nubank among younger, digital-first customers.

weaknesses: Falling behind Nubank and even its traditional peers in total customer count, with the lower-income 'mass market' segment increasingly ceded to lower-cost digital competitors

Minority-shareholder structure: ~90% owned by Santander Spain, leaving ADR holders exposed to related-party and capital-allocation decisions set by the controlling shareholder and limiting influence via the arbitration/By-Laws governance regime
Elevated and volatile cost of risk (3.7-3.8% annualized in 2025-2026) driven by wholesale one-offs, a rising-chapter-11 environment among Brazilian corporates, and high household indebtedness

Structurally lower efficiency ratio improvement than targeted (38-39% in late 2025/2026, worsening versus the 36-37% seen in early 2025) as market NII losses and provisioning volatility offset cost discipline
No reported U.S. GAAP reconciliation; financials are IFRS, adding a layer of accounting-standard risk/complexity for US investors versus domestic bank comparables

growth_drivers: Digital transformation and AI-driven hyper-personalization (OneApp multi-bank app, unified payments/Pix journey, AI-based data/analytics for origination and service) aimed at raising transactionality and NPS
SME expansion: expanded SME loan portfolio reached R$95 billion (+13% YoY) with a redesigned segmentation model for 2026 and continued investment in specialist coverage

Consumer Finance / auto lending ecosystem growth: loan portfolio of ~R$94-95 billion (+13% YoY), cross-selling (>1 million new accounts over two years), fast-growing attached insurance (+113% YoY) and fee generation

Fee income diversification away from credit-linked fees toward cards, insurance, asset management, consórcios and brokerage, explicitly framed by management as a 'key growth pillar' to reduce NII dependence
Funding mix improvement -- shifting toward lower-cost Individuals deposits (50-51% of funding mix, up ~4-5 points YoY) to reduce funding costs

Investment platform consolidation: integration of Toro Investimentos into Santander Corretora (announced 4Q25) to build a unified, scalable brokerage/wealth platform, including crypto-asset distribution
Sustainable finance: R$38.6 billion of sustainable business enabled and 41% market share in carbon-credit (CBIOS) issuance, supporting ESG-linked funding and corporate banking relationships

Secular tailwind: a multi-year Brazilian central-bank easing cycle (Selic forecast to fall toward ~13.5% by end-2026 and further to ~10% by 2029) should eventually support loan growth and ease funding costs, even though the bank reports near-term pain from rate sensitivity on its market NII book

business.description: Over-90-day NPL ratio rose to 3.7% (Dec-2025) and cost of risk to 3.76-3.81% through mid-2026, driven by lower-income individuals, SME stress and a rising number of corporate chapter-11-equivalent (recuperação judicial) filings; a change in write-off methodology and specific wholesale cases added a ~R$700 million one-off provision hit in Q2 2026.

Nubank has surpassed Bradesco (and nearly matches Itau) in customer count and continues to take share in payments and unsecured consumer credit; Santander has responded by deliberately shrinking exposure to the lower-income mass-market segment, trading customer growth for credit quality, which pressures Client NII spreads.

A large 'Market NII' book is directly exposed to interest-rate positioning and posted recurring losses in 2025-2026 (e.g., -R$1.5bn in 4Q25, -R$0.7bn in 2Q26), creating earnings volatility independent of the core lending franchise.

financial.description: The Brazilian real has historically shown large swings against the US dollar (from ~R$1.88/US$1 in 2011 to a low of R$4.195/US$1 in 2015, back to ~R$3.1-3.3 in 2016-2017, and further depreciation since); ADR holders bear this translation risk on top of underlying BRL earnings and equity even though BSBR itself manages FX exposure within the bank's own balance sheet.

financial.risk: Large non-operating FX/tax swings can distort reported income
financial.description: FY2020 is a clear precedent: 'Exchange differences (net)' swung to a R$24.7 billion loss (from a R$2.8 billion loss in 2019), depressing 'Total Income' to R$48.2 billion (from R$58.8 billion in 2019) even though net income held up, because a large offsetting income-tax benefit (a R$3.8 billion tax credit versus a R$5.6 billion tax expense in 2019) largely neutralized the hit at the net-income line. Analysts and the DCF should treat 2020 revenue/pre-tax income as not comparable without adjusting for this one-off FX/tax pairing.

financial.risk: Capital ratios and dividend/IoC distribution policy
financial.description: CET1 ratio was ~11.2-11.6% and BIS ratio ~15.0-15.4% through 2025-2026; the bank has maintained a steady quarterly interest-on-capital (IoC) distribution (R$1.5-2.0 billion per quarter, ~R$7.6 billion for all of 2025) but incremental earnings volatility (ROE down from 17.6% in 4Q25 to 12.5% in 2Q26) could pressure the sustainability of the payout ratio if not offset by capital release.

regulatory.description: CMN Resolution No. 4,966/21, adopted in 2025, reclassified certain origination/credit-related fees into net interest income and changed provisioning/renegotiated-portfolio definitions, breaking comparability of fee and cost-of-risk trends across 2024/2025 and requiring care when extrapolating growth rates.

regulatory.risk: Brazilian tax and dividend policy risk
regulatory.description: Proposed revocation of the income-tax exemption on dividends/interest-on-capital payments (a recurring legislative risk flagged in 20-F filings) could raise the effective tax cost of distributions to both Santander Spain and minority/ADR holders.

With Santander Spain holding ~89-90% of capital via Sterrebeeck B.V. and Grupo Empresarial Santander, related-party transactions, disputes are resolved via Brazilian arbitration (not US courts), and ADR holders vote only via instructions to the depositary -- all of which constrain minority shareholder influence relative to US domestic bank peers.

macro.risk: Selic rate policy and Brazilian macro cycle
macro.description: The majority of income, expenses, assets and liabilities are tied to interest rates; management estimated in the FY2020 20-F that a 1.0 percentage-point change in the Selic moves net interest income by roughly R$432 million. The current easing cycle (Selic forecast near 13.5% by end-2026, descending toward ~10% by 2029) could compress asset yields faster than funding costs reprice, even as it should eventually support credit growth and lower provisioning needs.

macro.risk: Brazilian political/fiscal instability and sovereign rating
macro.description: Brazil's sub-investment-grade sovereign rating (BB-/Ba2-area), chronic federal fiscal deficits since 2014, and episodic political shocks (e.g., Lava Jato-era investigations) have historically driven volatility in Brazilian asset prices and GDP growth, directly affecting loan demand and credit costs.

Elevated household indebtedness and a rising incidence of corporate insolvency filings are cited by management as a direct driver of the 2025-2026 cost-of-risk increase, particularly in SME and mass-income segments.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Brazilian banking remains a large, concentrated, and still-underpenetrated (relative to developed markets) credit market; the top five banks hold ~80% of system assets, but fintech disruption (led by Nubank) has materially reshaped the customer-acquisition and unsecured-credit/payments landscape over the past five years.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - Brazilian bank earnings are tightly linked to the Selic policy rate cycle, GDP growth, and credit/NPL cycles; BSBR's own disclosures show high sensitivity of NII and provisioning to macro swings
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Very high (direct) - both the asset/liability margin (NII) and provisioning costs move materially with Selic changes; management explicitly quantifies this sensitivity (a 1pp Selic move affects NII by several hundred million reais)
key_input_costs: Cost of funding (deposits, time deposits, wholesale funding)
Personnel costs (linked to annual union wage agreements, e.g. 5.68% in 2025)
Technology/IT investment (data processing, cloud, AI platforms)

recent_developments.event: Net profit of R$4.1 billion, highest quarterly profit in four years, ROAE 17.6% (stable QoQ, -0.1pp YoY); full-year 2025 net profit R$15.6 billion, +12.6% YoY; Toro Investimentos integrated into the Santander Corretora brand, including a move into crypto-asset distribution.
Recurring ROAE declined to 16.0% from 17.6% in 4Q25 as cost of risk and macro pressures began to build (per Q2-2026 release comparatives).

Recurring managerial net profit fell to R$3.0 billion (-20.4% QoQ, -17.6% YoY) with recurring ROAE dropping sharply to 12.5%; cost of risk rose to 3.81% (12-month annualized) including a ~R$700 million one-off from a change in write-off methodology plus specific wholesale provisioning cases; efficiency ratio deteriorated to 39.3%; management explicitly repositioned the book away from the mass-income segment toward higher-quality secured lending (mortgages, cards, Consumer Finance, SME), sacrificing near-term NII/customer growth for asset quality.

CEO succession: Mario Leao, CEO for 11 years, will step down by mid-2026 (expected July 2026); Gilson Finkelsztain, currently CEO of B3 (Brazil's stock exchange) and a former Santander Brasil executive, has been named as his successor pending regulatory approval. Outgoing management projected full-year 2026 profit to exceed the R$16.3 billion reported in the last full year under prior leadership, though Q1-Q2 2026 results (combined ~R$6.8 billion) suggest that bar is in doubt absent a strong H2 recovery.

Analyst sentiment has turned more cautious: JPMorgan downgraded BSBR to Neutral from Overweight (price target cut to $6 from $6.50) and HSBC maintained Hold (price target cut to $6.20 from $7.20) following the Q2 2026 profit miss and ROE guidance reset.

Nubank officially overtook Bradesco in Q1 2026 (per BACEN's quarterly customer ranking) to become Brazil's second-largest institution by customer base (~115 million customers, >60% of Brazil's adult population), intensifying competitive pressure on Santander Brasil's mass-market segment and informing its strategic pivot toward higher-income, secured lending.

Brazilian macro backdrop: Selic rate cuts resumed in 2026 after a prior tightening cycle; economists have trimmed the year-end 2026 Selic forecast toward ~13.5% as inflation cooled (2026 inflation estimate ~5.03%, fifth consecutive downward revision), with further easing projected to ~12% (2027), ~10.5% (2028) and ~10% (2029).

guidance.as_of: Q2 2026 earnings call / Q4 2025 earnings release

items.notes: Management reset expectations after the Q2 2026 ROAE drop to 12.5% (from 17.6% in 4Q25); guided ROE to remain in the 12-15% band through 2026 before a more material recovery expected in 2027, as the bank completes its deliberate shift toward higher-quality, secured lending.
Full-year 2026 total revenue growth guided to low single digits, reflecting the mass-market de-risking strategy and market NII volatility; meaningful recovery pushed into 2027.

Management characterizes recent cost-of-risk increases as including identifiable one-offs (write-off methodology change, specific wholesale cases totaling ~R$700 million in 2Q26) layered on a 'still challenging' macro backdrop; expects discipline and portfolio repositioning to gradually improve credit quality.

Consistent quarterly interest-on-capital distributions of R$1.5-2.0 billion maintained through the ROE downturn (R$2.0bn approved for both March and June 2026 quarters), suggesting management views the capital base (CET1 ~11.2%, BIS ~15.3%) as sufficient to sustain the payout despite lower near-term earnings.

items.target: continued cost discipline, ratio near-term pressured to ~38-39%
items.vs_prior: lowered (worse than the ~36-37% seen in early 2025)
items.notes: Expenses have been held below inflation (general expenses +2.6% YoY in 2Q26) but the efficiency ratio has deteriorated mechanically due to softer/volatile revenue, particularly negative market NII.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mario Leao (through Q4 2025) emphasized 'consistent ROAE evolution' and confidence that 2026 full-year profit would exceed the R$16.3 billion reported under his tenure's final full year, driven by Consumer Finance, SME and investment-platform momentum. By Q2 2026, management's tone shifted to acknowledging a deliberate near-term profitability sacrifice: CFO Gustavo Alejo and incoming leadership described a strategy of 'selective and balanced asset growth' and 'disciplined capital allocation,' explicitly trading mass-market revenue/customer growth for a more resilient, secured loan book, with ROE guided to stay in the 12-15% range through 2026 and a 'more material' recovery expected only in 2027 as repositioning completes and Selic easing feeds through to funding costs.

dcf_notes_for_analyst.method: Bank - use FCFE at cost of equity (per scripts/schema.py / dcf-methods convention), not a free-cash-flow/EBITDA growth DCF. Equity value should be built off BVPS-compounding or an excess-return/FCFE-at-CoE framework, net_debt should be treated as not meaningful for a bank, and distributions (IoC + dividends) should anchor the payout assumption.
dcf_notes_for_analyst.net_interest_margin_direction: Client NII spread has been compressing (10.67% in 4Q25, down to 10.03% in 2Q26) due to a deliberate mix shift away from the higher-margin, higher-risk mass-income segment toward secured/higher-quality lending (mortgages, cards, Consumer Finance, SME); Market NII has been a recurring drag (losses of R$1.0-1.5bn/quarter through most of 2025-2026) tied to interest-rate positioning, though it showed sequential improvement in 2Q26 as the securities portfolio matured. Base case should assume NIM stabilizes/modestly recovers as Selic easing reduces funding costs and the repositioned book reprices, but near-term (2026) spread compression should not be extrapolated as a permanent trend.
dcf_notes_for_analyst.credit_cost_trend: Cost of risk rose from ~3.7% (late 2025) to ~3.8% (mid-2026), including identifiable one-off items (~R$700 million from a write-off methodology change and specific wholesale cases in 2Q26). NPL ratios (over-90-day) have drifted up to ~3.7% as of Dec-2025 / 3.3% by Jun-2026 (post methodology change, not directly comparable), concentrated in lower-income individuals and SME/corporate segments amid elevated household indebtedness and a rising incidence of corporate insolvency. Analysts should model an elevated but normalizing cost of risk in 2026-2027 as the deliberate portfolio de-risking (away from mass-market) takes effect, with full normalization more likely by 2027.
dcf_notes_for_analyst.roe_trajectory: ROE peaked at 17.6% in 4Q25 (stable vs 4Q24) before falling sharply to 16.0% in 1Q26 and 12.5% in 2Q26 due to the combination of spread compression and elevated credit provisions. Management guidance: ROE to remain in a 12-15% range through FY2026, with a 'more material' recovery targeted for FY2027 as the repositioning (mass-market exit, secured-lending mix shift, Selic easing pass-through) completes. A multi-year DCF should model a trough-to-recovery ROE path (e.g., ~13-14% average 2026, climbing toward high-teens by 2028-2029) rather than extrapolating either the 2025 peak or the 2026 trough.
dcf_notes_for_analyst.capital_return_policy: BSBR distributes interest-on-capital (IoC) and dividends quarterly rather than via buybacks; recent quarterly IoC distributions have been R$1.5-2.0 billion (R$7.62 billion approved across all distributions for FY2025), maintained through the 2026 ROE downturn, implying management is willing to let the payout ratio rise temporarily rather than cut the nominal distribution. CET1 ~11.2-11.6% and BIS ~15.0-15.4% provide some cushion. Model dividends/IoC as the primary capital-return channel, with a payout ratio that may compress retained-earnings-driven book-value growth below net income growth in a FCFE-at-CoE framework.
one_off_items_to_normalize: FY2020: 'Exchange differences (net)' FX loss of R$24.7 billion (vs R$2.8 billion in FY2019), largely offset by an income tax benefit swinging to +R$3.8 billion (from a R$5.6 billion expense in FY2019); net effect was a depressed 'Total Income'/pre-tax line in FY2020 (R$48.2bn vs R$58.8bn in FY2019) despite broadly stable net income (R$13.4bn). Treat FY2020 revenue growth as not representative of underlying trend.
Q2 2026: ~R$700 million one-off provisioning hit from a change in write-off methodology plus specific wholesale banking cases, embedded in the reported 20.6% QoQ jump in result from loan losses.

2025: CMN Resolution No. 4,966/21 reclassified certain origination-related fees into NII and changed provisioning/renegotiated-portfolio definitions, breaking YoY comparability of the fee line and cost-of-risk metric starting FY2025; management disclosed that, excluding this effect, FY2025 fees would have grown ~6.9% YoY versus the ~4.3% reported.

bull_case: Deep-pocketed, globally diversified parent (Santander Group) provides technology, risk-management and funding support unavailable to standalone domestic peers, and has signaled long-term commitment to the Brazilian franchise

Consistent, maintained quarterly capital returns (IoC/dividends, ~R$2.0 billion/quarter) even through the 2026 earnings downturn, offering income support for ADR holders while the turnaround plays out

Multi-year Brazilian rate-easing cycle (Selic trending from mid-teens toward ~10% by 2029) should eventually lower funding costs and support loan growth and NIM once the bank's own portfolio repositioning is complete

Deliberate, disclosed strategy of trading near-term mass-market growth for higher asset quality (secured lending, SME, Consumer Finance) should reduce credit-cost volatility and set up a credible ROE recovery toward/above 15%+ by 2027 per management's own framing

New CEO (Gilson Finkelsztain, ex-Santander Brasil and current B3 chief) brings fresh perspective and capital-markets expertise, potentially accelerating the investment-platform (Santander Corretora/Toro) and digital strategy
bear_case: Structural share loss to Nubank and other digital challengers (Nubank now larger than Bradesco by customer count, >60% Brazilian adult penetration) threatens Santander Brasil's long-term retail franchise and pricing power, especially in payments and unsecured credit

Sharp, recent ROE deterioration (17.6% in 4Q25 to 12.5% in 2Q26) and management's own guidance of a 12-15% ROE band through all of FY2026 signal a multi-quarter earnings trough with execution risk around whether the 2027 recovery materializes as planned

High sensitivity to Brazilian macro/political risk and BRL volatility: sub-investment-grade sovereign rating, chronic fiscal deficits, and history of sharp currency swings (as in 2015 and 2020) create outsized, hard-to-hedge risk for USD-based ADR holders versus BRL-denominated earnings and equity

Minority-shareholder governance structure (~89-90% owned by Santander Spain) limits ADR holders' influence over capital allocation, related-party transactions, and strategic decisions, and the group could in principle subordinate Brazilian minority interests to broader group priorities

Elevated and volatile cost of risk, including recurring 'one-off' wholesale provisioning charges and a structurally pressured market NII book, make near-term earnings difficult to forecast and raise the risk that credit costs stay structurally higher than pre-2025 levels given Brazil's elevated household indebtedness
